People respond differently to eating plans. Experiment to find the best combination of food and activity that works for you. Set yourself up for success If you're like many people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, weight loss is part of your treatment plan. It sounds so simple: eat less and move more. But if weight loss were that easy, millions of people wouldn't be struggling right now to do it. And you've probably noticed that even people who take the weight off have a hard time keeping it off. More and more studies show that people respond differently to diets. For example, some lose weight on low carb; some gain weight. The same goes for other plans. So how do you find your secret sauce for weight loss? Make sure to focus on healthy, nutritious food. pages.text: Welcome Baseball Fans! | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Welcome Baseball Fans! If you're a fan of baseball and disability employment, you've come to the right place! At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. pages.text: Welcome to Shuttle-Mir Come along with the seven U.S. astronauts and all the cosmonauts that called Mir their home, and visit the sights and sounds of the Shuttle-Mir Program CD-ROM! Tour the Russian Space Station with the STS missions that took the residents to Mir and brought them back to Earth. View hundreds of photos , videos , diagrams , as well as computer generated animations of the Mir deorbit , collision , and flyaround . Read mission status reports, published documents, news releases, personal letters, oral histories of some of the people who made the Shuttle-Mir Program successful, and much more . Learn about the science that was performed on Mir and the important results of those experiments . See the Shuttle-M i r book online and search the entire site for information. Wellbore Construction and Evaluation Wellbores are a critical component of the infrastructure and success of geothermal electricity generation projects and represent a significant hurdle for developers. Improving the durability and costs of wellbore structures and ensuring long-term well flow are vital to reduce costs and ensure safe, efficient operation of geothermal power plants. The Office of Geothermal is funding projects that can support these needs for both next-generation and conventional geothermal systems. Wells of Opportunity A key step to unlocking the full potential of reliable, domestic geothermal energy may lie inside millions of American oil and gas wells . These wells can be used to harness geothermal energy in two ways: through the retrofitting of inactive or unproductive wells, or through co-production on active wells. Well Retrofits In well retrofits, an unused, dry, or unproductive oil and gas well first undergoes any repairs necessary for safe operation. Water is then pumped into the oil and gas well, where it is warmed by the earth and drawn back to the surface to power a thermoelectric generator. The hot water pulled to the surface can be used for heating, cooling, or to power nearby structures and homes. America has millions of dry or unproductive oil and gas wells, many of which could be retrofitted for geothermal use. Note: The scope of the Office of Geothermal’s WOO initiative specifically targets inactive or unproductive wells. When ancient humans interbred, new research shows that the pairings were predominantly male Neanderthals and female Homo sapiens. Daynes/Science Photo Library By Annie Roth Published February 26, 2026 Neanderthal men may have had a thing for modern human women, or perhaps Neanderthal men had something human women couldn't resist. That’s one potential interpretation of a new study, published Thursday in Science , that found when Neanderthals and Homo sapiens interbred, the pairings were predominantly between Neanderthal men and human women. Scientists have long known that some of our ancestors reproduced with Neanderthals before the species went extinct roughly 40,000 years ago. Today, traces of Neanderthal DNA linger in the genomes of many people, particularly among those with non-African ancestry. On average, it amounts to about one to two percent of a person’s genome. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. A renowned statistician, he’d retired from his teaching post at the University of California Berkeley. “We thought it was anxiety or depression,” says his daughter, Liz Selvin. Selvin’s behavior—easily mistaken for other mental health issues because it changed gradually—was a symptom of dementia. The professor was adept at concealing his growing cognitive impairment—until he couldn’t, Liz says. Her dad began letting strangers into the house. He repeated himself. Actually, no: An Earth day isn’t a fixed interval of time. You may have noticed news stories reporting that Earth has shaved a millisecond (thousandth of a second) or more off the time it takes to make a full rotation, or conversely, that the planet’s rotation has slowed down slightly. While some of these stories exaggerate the impacts of these changes, their basic premise is correct: Earth’s seemingly steady rotation can, at times, seem as fickle as the weather. Christie's Images, Bridgeman Images By Sarah Bond Published September 14, 2026 In August of 29 B.C., Octavian, the adopted son of Julius Caesar, held an opulent triumphal procession within the city of Rome. The 33-year-old was the ultimate victor in a long struggle for control of the Roman Empire, and to commemorate his victory, the new emperor held a three-day parade in celebration of his defeat of Marc Antony and Cleopatra and acquisition of Egypt. During the triumph, Octavian marched two children of the ill-fated pair through the streets of Rome as living spoils of war: The ten-year-old twins Cleopatra Selene and Alexander Helios. Octavian had wanted to display the vanquished Egyptian herself to the thousands of Romans that lined the streets. Illustration by Dominic Bodden Whatever happened to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s tradition of fireside chats? Frances Gelles | Denver The spread of radio gave Roosevelt the means to have his speeches broadcast into listeners’ homes in real time, through relatively informal messages he called fireside chats. But while Roosevelt was the first to be able to employ this approach on a large scale, he was not the last. Every president since then has found ways to use the media of their day to deliver personal, conversational messages directly to the public. Jimmy Carter once gave a televised “fireside chat” while sitting by an actual White House fireplace. Ronald Reagan didn’t use the fireside title or motif, but he did deliver radio addresses to the public each Saturday. Barack Obama was the first president to communicate with the public through social media, a practice carried on by his successors, Donald Trump and Joe Biden. The title and medium may have changed, but the spirit of the presidential fireside chat lives on. — Claire Jerry, curator of political history, National Museum of American History What are the factors that limit the altitude a housefly can reach?
